Development of NH Nos. 57 and 57-A 
†*482. SHRI MANGANI LAL MANDAL: Will the Mipister of 
SHIPPING, ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that a length of about 7300 kilometers of National 
Highways is being developed as PSEW corridor and built into a four lane 
highway. 
(b) whether it is also a fact that the process of construction is 
proceeding at a snail's pace; 
(c) whether it is a fact that there is little change in the status with regard 
to National Highway Nos. 57 and 57-A on East-West corridor; and 
(d) if so, the details of the latest position with regard to the above three 
stretches? 
THE MINISTER OF SHIPPI NG, ROAD TRANSPORT AND 
HIGHWAYS (SHRI T.R. BAALU): (a) to (d) A Statement is laid on the Table 
of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. However, name of the corridor is North South and East West 
(NS-EW) corridor. 
(b) No, Sir. Out of 7300 km length of North-South and East-West 
Corridor, 981 km has been approved under National Highways Development 
Project Phase-I and remaining length under National Highways Development 
ProjectPhase-ll. 822 km of highways under North South & East West Corridors 
have been 4-laned under National Highways Development Project Phase-I. In 
National Highways Development Project Phase-ll, the work has been awarded 
for 4892 kms, and most of these have been recently awarded. Nearly 232 km of 
corridor needs realignment due to wild life forest, 318 km is mountainous and 
difficult terrain in Jammu and Kashmir. All works in remaining stretches are likely 
to be awarded by September 2006. 
(c) and (d) NH-57 from Muzaffarpur to Purnia forms part of East West 
Corridor. All civil work contracts on the stretch have already been awarded. 
Forbesganj-Jogbani Section of NH-57A has been entrusted to

(f) whether the construction is meeting the international standards; and 
(g) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (g) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House.

RAJYA SABHA [18 May, 2006] 
Statement 
(a) and (b) The preparation/training of sportspersons for major 
international events including Commonwealth Games is an on-going process 
which takes into account inputs provided by National Sports Federations. A 
systematic approach is adopted to se lect and train athletes and teams for 
participation in major international events by drawing up Long Term 
Development Programmes (LTDP) to put in action four year roll-on Plan under 
which exceptionally talented sportspersons, selected on the basis of their 
performance, are put through scientifically designed continuous training 
programmes. 
(c) As at present, no specific funds have been allocated for imparting 
training to Indian Teams for the Commonwealth Games, 2010. However, in 
order to achieve better results in Commonwealth Games, 2010, Government 
is holding discussions with the Organizing Committee Commonwealth 
Games, 2010, the Sports Authority of India and various National Sports 
Federations to identify areas to provide substantially enhanced assistance for 
the training of promising sportspersons who could win medals for the 
country. 
(d) and (e) The Core Group of Ministers (GOM) for coordinating the work 
related to Commonwealth Games, 2010 has recommended the venues for 
various events of Commonwealth Games, 2010 and desired that the respective 
agencies should proceed with the process of concept plan and design on the basis 
of global tendering, following the established due procedure for financial 
sanction. The work of actual construction would start on the completion of 
these processes. 
(f) and (g) Do not arise in view of the answer to (d) and (e) above. 
SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY; Sir, the question is 
pertaining to the Commonwealth Games. Hosting the Commonwealth Games 
is a prestigious issue for the nation. Preparations and construction of stadia and 
laying of tracks should meet the international standards. I would like to seek 
Some clarifications from the hon. Minister. Part (1) of my question is: What 
are the steps taken in this regard? Part (2) of my question is that already some 
infrastructure of international standard is available in Hyderabad. I would like 
to know whether you are going to utilise that infrastructure which was 
constructed for National Games and Afro-Asian Games. You must have seen 
it for yourself. I would like to 
20 

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
know whether you would allocate certain events to Hyderabad and utilise this 
infrastructure of high standards. 
SHRIMANISHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, the Commonwealth Games are not 
awarded to a nation; they are awarded to a city and it was city of Delhi which 
competed against the city of Hamilton in Canada to secure the Games. At the 
time when the flag was handed over to us, it was not handed over to the 
Union Minister of Sports but to the Chief Minister of Delhi. Hence, although ! 
fully recognise that there are excellent sports facilities available in Hyderabad 
and it will be desirable for us to utilse those for international sports 
competitions, in this specific case of the Commonwealth Games there is no 
alternative but to concentrate all activities here in Delhi. 
SHRI RAVULACHANDRASEKAR REDDY: Sir, my second question is 
regarding training to the sports persons. Often we hear that politics take place 
while selecting the players. What are the special steps taken in containing the 
interference by politicians in sports  activities? There is an accepted 
international phrase "catch them young". Now we have the latest controversy of 
Budhia of Orissa. Since the internationally accepted phrase is "catch them 
young" what is the policy of the Government and what is the thinking cf the 
Government, as far as this controversy is concerned? What are the steps 
taken in selecting the players for the Commonwealth Games and giving 
training to them? How much is the money allocated for this purpose? 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, my congratulations to the hon. 
Member on including six questions within one question. I will do my best to 
answer what he has asked. 
SHRI RAVULACHANDRASEKAR REDDY: I have asked for them. 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: In so far as preventing the selection 
process from being polluted by political interference, I can assure the hon. 
Member that we will not listen to any political interference in this matter, not 
even from Chandra Sekar Reddygaru. We will ensure that the selection is kept 
as non-polluted by Members of this House or other politicians as we possible 
can. 
In regard to the training, we have, at the present moment, three major 
sources of funding the training. One is a scheme under which assistance is 
given to National Sports Federations and much of the 
21 

RAJYA SABHA [18 May, 2006] 
responsibility for selecting, looking into this and checking whether the work 
is being done is with the National Sports Federations, although the responsibility 
for training vests substantially in the Sports Authority of India. The second source 
of this is a scheme called the Talent Search and Training Scheme. Under that, 
we look for talented sports persons and try to nurture them to international 
standards. The third is the National S ports Fund where it was hoped that the 
Corporate India would want to make its contribution to 'India Shining', but I am 
very, very sad to inform this House that the corporate sector in India has not risen 
to the expectations on the basis of which this National Sports Fund was 
established. I do hope that as a result of the opportunity given to me here to bring 
this matter up, we will see greater awareness on the part of corporate India that 
since these sports events do indeed generate huge business opportunities, 
business itself should come forward to assist in making these activities reach 
international standards. On our part, we have got the Organising Committee 
of the games which makes suggestion in this regard. We have the Apex 
Committee which looks into proposals that come from the Organising Committee 
or elsewhere. We are hoping that through a normal process of going to the 
empowered Finance Committee and later if required to the Cabinet 
Committee on Economic Affairs, we will be able to get additional funding, if 
required and as estimated by the technical authorities concerned to give 
special training in the context of the Comonwealth Games. But above all, in 
my view, unless we spread our net very wide, unless we go beyond urban elite 
institutions, and we go beyond accidental discovery of sports talent in rural 
India, until we make a systematic way to reach out to approximately 37 crore 
children, adolescents and young persons who are at the present moment not 
exposed to formal sports, we would not be able to really tap the vast mine of 
talent that exists in this country. Towards this end, I am hoping that we will 
secure permission for and bring to the attention of this House a Panchayati Raj 
Yuva Shakti Khelkood Abhiyan.

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the people in slum clusters in metropolitan cities specially in 
Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai are living in miserable conditions; 
(b) whether Government propose to take any effective steps to provide 
necessary basic amenities like power, pollution free environment, severage, 
drinking water to the people living in such slum clusters in the country, 
specially in Delhi; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
to (c) A Statement is laid on the Table of the Sabha. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The slum clusters in metropolitan cities including Delhi, 
Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai do in deed lack sufficient basic civic 
amenities. For integrated Development of slums through projects for 
providing shelter, basic services and other civic amenities with a view to 
provide utilities to the urban poor in select 63 cities, a Sub-Mission on Basic 
Services to the Urban Poor (BSUP) has been launched on 3rd December, 
2005. Delhi, Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai are included in these 63 cities. The 
Sub-Mission on BSUP is implemented on a demand-driven basis for which State 
Governments are required to prepare and submit City Development Plans 
(CDPs); Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) and also to sign Memorandum of 
Agreement (MoA) making a commitment to undertake urban reforms. Major 
admissible components of BSUP inter-alia include housing; environmental 
improvement and development of infrastructure projects; construction and 
improvement of drains/storm water drains; solid waste management; street 
lighting; improvement of water supply/sewerage/drainage; construction of 
community toilets/baths; providing civic amenities like community halls, child 
care centres, etc. However, providing electric power is not an admissible 
component.

activities.

THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL 
REDDY): (a) to (c) The planned development of Delhi is governed by the 
provisions of the Master Plan, as notified by the Central Government under the 
Delhi Development Act 1957. The Master Plan provides, inter-alia. for 
different categories of land uses, such as, residential, commercial, public 
facilities, recreational and the like. It also provides for mixed use activity, 
such as, use of residential land for non-residential purposes. 
Delhi has witnessed rapid growth in population in the last few decades. 
This has resulted in demand for different categories of land uses far 
outstripping its supply. This has been one of the major causes of reported 
violations of the land use provisions of the Plan in Delhi. 
To meet the emerging requirements of Delhi, Master Plan provisions are 
amended from time to time. Extensive modifications are at present being 
undertaken in the Master Plan of Delhi 2001. In the proposed Master Plan of Delhi 
2021, more realistic and flexible land use policies are being proposed, which 
include—private participation in land development, more liberal norms for 
development control and mixed land use policy.

contracts.

heat value (UHV) to the international practice of pricing coal based 
on gross calorific value (GCV). Th is is expected to encourage 
efficient use and promote use of washed coal.

1970 to facilitate offloading of certain activities in coal mining for

(  For Telephone Companies:

Statement 
Germany-India Joint Statement issued on the occasion of the Visit of Prime 
Minister Dr. Manmohan Singh to Germany 23/04/2006 
Federal Chancellor Angela Merkel and Prime Minister Manmohan Singh 
today reaffirmed the Strategic Partnership of Germany and India. Building 
upon the 'Agenda for the Indo-German Partnership in the 21st Century', 
which both countries adopted in the year 2000, Germany and India will deepen 
their strategic partnership based on shared democratic values and basic 
common interests. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [18 May, 2006] 
The Indo-German Strategic Partnership has seen co-operation 
intensifying across the board, including on the G4 initiative relating to the reform 
of the United Nations Security Council. Both sides agree to continue co-operation 
bilaterally and in the framework of G4 for the strengthening of the multilateral 
system and a reform of the United Nations, including the reform of the UN 
Security Council. 
Trade, investment, scientific and technological collaboration, including 
in the areas of infrastructure, energy and high technology areas such as space, 
form an important basis for the partnership. Both sides aim to further deepen 
their strategic and security dialogue and will work towards an agreement on 
bilateral defence co-operation. 
Economic and trade relations between Germany and India have 
flourished in recent years. India's partic ipation as the Partner Country in this 
year's Hannover Messe reflects the growing interest in India as a global 
economic partner and offers an excellent opportunity to intensify bilateral 
economic ties, Infrastructure and Energy  provide major areas of deepening 
engagement between the two countries. The Indo-German Joint Commission on 
Industrial and Economic Co-operation will continue to focus on specific areas of 
co-operation for mutual benefit. Both sides note with satisfaction that bilateral 
trade is growing rapidly and that the target of doubling the trade within five 
years, which was set at the previous Summit meeting in New Delhi in 
October 2004 is likely to be achieved much earlier. Both sides recognize the 
significant role of the small and medium enterprises in further promoting the 
trade, investment and technology links and agree to facilitate intensification of 
linkages of such enterprises. They also note with appreciation, the 
contribution of the Indo-German Chamber of Commerce, which is celebrating 
its 50th anniversary this year, to promote economic co-operation between the 
two countries. They welcome the opening of a German Trade Office in 
Bangalore, which will further promote German trade and investment in India. 
They also welcome the growing trend of Indian investments in Germany. 
In this context both sides commend the work of the Indo-German 
Consultative Group and welcome their recommendations for further 
strengthening of our overall relationship including our economic and trade ties. 
94 

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Both sides acknowledge the valuable contributions of Indo-German 
development co-operation in wide-ranging areas including energy, 
environmental policy, sustainable economic development, health and 
vocational training. 
The establishment of an Indo-German Energy Forum at Senior Officials 
level and including the private sector highlights the importance accorded by 
both countries to co-operate in this sector. The Energy Forum will address strategic 
energy concerns including energy security, efficient use of energy, promotion of 
renewable energy sources and environmentally friendly technologies, taking 
into account the environmental challenges of sustainable development. 
The two sides also take note of the satisfactory progress being made 
with regard to co-operation between the EU and India in the energy sector and 
the fact that the India-EU Joint Action Plan finalized in September 2005 at 
the 6th EU-lndia Summit in New Delhi, provides for co-operation on achieving 
safe, secure, affordable and sustainable energy supplies. India's participation in the 
ITER initiative on fusion energy is an important part of the ongoing energy co-
operation. 
Germany and India have established a long and fruitful co-operation in 
Science and Technology. The Indo-Germ an Science Circle has given new 
impetus to this co-operation and will further strengthen contacts between 
scientific and academic communities. Both sides expect that the newly 
established office of the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft in New Delhi will 
further add to the close network of institutions between our two countries. Both 
sides will work towards setting up an Indo-German Science, Research and 
Technology Centre at an early date. The Indian Council for Medical Research 
and the Helmohltz Association of German research centres are signing an MoU 
on Research Co-operation in the field of biomedical sciences. 
Germany will place special emphasis on co-operation in Science and 
Technology between Germany and India during its Presidency of the European 
Union. Both sides will work towards jointly organizing a Ministerial 
conference on Science and Technology in the first half of 2007. 
Both sides take a note of the ongoing bilateral co-operation in the space 
sector including in the Chandrayaan project. India's participation

in the Global Navigation Satellite System (GALILEO) will be an 
important contribution to such co-operation.

Relaxation in the visa policy 
3529 KUMARI NIRMALA DESHPANDE: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state 
(a) whether mspite of the continuing peace process between India and 
Pakistan there is no relaxation in the visa policy, which is the main road block 
in people to people contacts; 
(b) whether the Ministry rs planning to give relaxation unilaterally to the 
senior citizens, who are keen to visit their birth place; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI E. AHAMMED): (a) Government firmly believes that 
100 

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
people to people contact is a significant factor in generating goodwill.and 
promoting bilateral relations between India and Pakistan, and it has 
consistently endeavoured to negotiate a visa regime that encourages such 
contacts. In keeping with this policy, Government announced unilateral visa 
liberalizations in September 2004, which included, inter alia, multiple entry 
visas for accredited journalists, exemption from reporting to the police for 
various categories of Pakistani nationals such as those above 65 years of age, 
academicians, and doctors. In December 2004, Government a nnounced 
additional visa liberalization measures such as visa on arrival at Wagah for 
certain categories of people and grant of student visas for allowing admission 
in Indian institutions to Pakistani students on a case-by-case basis. 
India presented a draft proposing amendments to the present India-Pakistan 
Visa Agreement during the visit of former Extenal Affairs Minister to Pakistan 
from 2-5 October 2005. The draft envisages longer duration visit visas for 
people from both countries and proposes the addition of new categories of 
visas such as student, pilgrims and business visa to facilitate easier movement 
of people across the border. Pakistan has not given its response to this draft visa 
agreement. Talks on visa matters are continuing in the third round of the India-
Pakistan Composite Dialogue. 
(b) and (c) With regard to seni or citizens, on 18 September 2004, 
Government had announced unilaterally the grant of visas with exemption from 
reporting to the Police to all Pakistani nationals above the age of 65. 
Government unilaterally announced visa on arrival to be available at Wagah for 
Pakistani nationals above the age of 65 during the Forein Secretary level talks 
held on 27 December 2004. Pakistan, however, does not allow its citizens to 
come to the Wagah check-post without a visa for India.

(c) and (d) All the advertisements/p rogrammes of satellite TV channels 
transmitted or re-transmitted through cable service are required to adhere to the 
provisions of the Advertising Code and Programme Code prescribed under the 
Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, 1995 and rules framed 
thereunder. The Central Government ha s constituted an Inter-Ministerial 
Committee under Section 20 of the Act to look into the violation of the 
Programme Code and Advertising Code. The Committee either suo-moto or 
on receipt of complaint, examines cases of violations of the code. Show cause 
notices are issued in the first instance to TV chanels telecasting objectionable 
advertisements in violation of code and TV channels are directed not to 
telecast/re-telecast the advertisement, which are found to be violative of the 
Advertising Code. So far 57 Show Cause Notices have been issued in 2006 upto 
15.05.2006. This is an ongoing process. Government has issued an order on 
6th September, 2005 for constitution of Monitoring Committees at the State 
and district levels to monitor private satellite TV channels and local cable 
channels to detect and look into violations of the Programme and Advertising 
Code and complaints received from general public regarding violation of the 
Code. As per the Ministry of Women and Child Development which 
administers the Indecent Representation of Women (Prohibition) Act, 1986, there 
is negative depiction of the image of women in print media. As per section 3 and 
4 of the Act, publishing of obscene/ indecent portrayal of women is a punishable 
offence. Under the Act, an officer de signated by the State Government is 
empowered to take action in instances of its violation. Further, the Press 
Council, a statuory autonomous body, set up under the Press Council Act, 1978 
with the twin object of preserving the freedom of the press and of maintaining 
and improving the standards of newspapers and news agencies in India has also 
laid down "Norms of Journalistic Conduct" stipulating for obscenity and 
vulgarity to be eschewed. 
Conditions of overseas Indians 
3551. DR. K.MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of OVERSEAS INDIAN 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) the living and economic conditions of overseas Indians in general and 
the working class in particular; 
(b) whether the overseas Indians are treat ed as second class citizens in 
the social status; 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [18 May, 2006] 
(c) whether there is a silent move to discourage the inflow of Indians 
abroad and get employed; 
(d) whether it is a fact that overseas Indians are not employed in certain 
category of employment irrespective of their merit, qualification and fitness; 
and 
(e) the initiative to make a thorough study of the various problems of 
Indians abroad and the measures proposed to be taken to correct such burning 
issues faced by them? 
THE MINISTER OF OVERSEAS INDIAN AFFAIRS (SHRI 
VAYALAR RAVI): (a) and (b) Over the years, overseas Indians in general have 
prospered socially and economically in their respective countries of domicile. 
NRI/PIOs have gained political and economic prominence in several 
countries such as USA, UK and Canada. Overseas Indians are recognized for 
their technical skills, knowledge and expertise in frontier technologies such as 
information technology and bio-technology. Overseas Indian workers are 
estimated at between 4 to 5 million with an annual gross flow of half a million 
workers excluding returnees. These workers are mostly semi/un-skilled and are 
appreciated for their sincerity, hard work and non-interference abroad. The 
remittances by overseas Indian worker s into India are estimated at $12-15 
billion annually. The largest numbers of overseas Indian workers are in the 
Gulf countries and are mainly in the unorganized sector. Since they are not 
covered by local labour laws, there are instances of workers being subjected to 
long working hours, non-payment of wages, poor working conditions etc. When 
such instances are reported, steps are taken by our Missions to redress the 
grievances of the workers. 
(c) and (d) While there is no overt move by foreign Governments to check 
the inflow of Indians to their countries, barriers have been raised through strict 
immigration/visa procedures, excessive checks and control in their travel to and 
stay in the host country. 
(e) A separate Ministry, i.e. the Ministry of Overseas Indian Affairs has 
been created to look after the affairs of Indians abroad which works in tandem 
with the Ministry of External Affairs to address the problems and concerned of 
overseas Indians. Besides comprehensive amendment to the Emigration Act, 
other measures including the streamlining of the emigration process through 
E-governance and a publicity campaign to 
126

obligations will be initiated.

Confederation of Indian Industries (CM) are working together to facilitate 
building linkages between Panchayats, industries and businesses to create 
Rural Business Hubs (RBH) in different blocks of the country on the lines of 
the successful Thai experience of One Tambon One Product (OTOP). Rural 
Business Hubs are proposed to be Public-Private-Panchayat Partnerships to

Rural Business Hubs (RBH) will be promoted on the basis of Memoranda of 
Understanding (MOU) between key stakeholders for ensuring development 
of the RBH in a set time frame, covering  every facet of product development, 
ensuring quality, value addition, market access and securing better prices. 
Under the Rural Business Hubs initiative, 31 MOUs have so far been signed 
between Panchayats and Corporates in the public and private sectors and 73 
business houses located by the Cll have expressed their interests in further 
exploring the prospects for specific RBH.

Gram Sabhas 
3557. SHRI SHANTARAM LAXMAN NAIK: Will the Minister of 
PANCHAYATI RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to recommend to the State 
Government any changes in the matter of holdings Gram Sabhas; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
134 

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether any study with respect to the functioning of Gram Sabhas in the 
country has been made after new regime of panchayat system become 
operational after 73rd Constitutional amendment? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR): (a) to (c) Article 243-A of the Constitution provides for the 
establishment of Gram Sabhas to "exercise such powers and perform such 
functions at the village level as the Legislature of a State may, by law 
provide". During the Round Table M eeting of the State Ministers of 
Panchayati Raj held in Kolkata in July 2004, it was decided that State 
Governments may review the extant legislation to determine the legislative 
and other steps needed to be taken to ensure that the powers and functions 
mentioned in Article 243 A are adequately incorporated in the State 
legislation. These include constitution of Sabhas below the Gram level such as 
Gram Sansad or Ward Sabha, periodicity of meetings of Gram Sabhas and 
Ward Sabhas and empowering the Gram Sabha with measures such as right to 
all information required to make the Panchayats truly answerable to the Gram 
Sabha, approval of plans prepared by the Gram Panchayat, issue of utilization 
certificates of funds allocated for the plans, programmes of the Panchayat and 
identification of beneficiaries. Though no nation-wide study has been 
undertaken, there are reports of low attendance in Gram Sabhas and 
infrequency of meetings. 
An Expert Group constituted by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj on 
planning at the grass roots level has submitted its report in March 2006 which 
has been accepted by the Ministry. Some of the recommendations of the Group 
relate to participative planning at the Gram Panchayat level and it has been 
suggested in this context that certain steps should be carried out on a campaign 
mode to ensure good participation in  Gram Sabhas and Ward Sabhas. These 
include advance notice of meetings, mobilization of special interest groups 
such as self-help groups for attending the Word and Gram Sabhas, campaigns 
through National Survey Scheme and Nehru Yuvak kendra Volunteers, 
nomination of facilitators for each Ward  Sabha and having a proper structure 
for the Gram and Ward Sabha and having a proper structure for the Gram and 
Ward Sabha with scope to break up into smaller groups for discussion.

Investment to improve the economy 
3572. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided the decade ahead to turn into 
one of investment to covert the nation into a first-rate agricultural, industrial 
and service economy; and 
(b) if so, the steps taken in this direction so far.?. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) The Tenth Five Year Plan aims 
at doubling of the per capita income in time-span of a decade. For the 
pursuance of this goal, the Tenth Five Year Plan had aimed for accelerating 
the growth rate in the years to come in agricultural, industrial and services 
sectors. In order to achieve the accelera ted growth rates, the Plan aimed at 
raising savings and investment rates in the Plan. As a result, the savings and 
investment rates in economy have increased from 23.6% and 23.0% 
respectively, in 2001-02 to 29.1% and 30.1%, respectively in 2004-05, the 
latest year for which the information is 
148 

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
available. Both the Tenth Five Year Plan and the Mid-term Appraisal (MTA) of the 
Tenth Plan have suggested a number of measures to raise the growth rate in the 
country. Some of these include raising public investment in different sectors 
particularly in agriculture, infrastructure, viz. power, roads, greater focus on 
health and education, improving allocative efficiency of resources, enacting 
policy .eforms with a view to creating an investor friendly environment, 
improving governance and enhancing the efficiency of delivery systems, etc. A 
large number of new programmes like Accelerated Irrigation Benefit 
Programme, Accelerated Power Development Programme, Bharat Nirman 
Programme, National Highway Development Programme and National Urban 
Renewal Mission have been launched to achieve accelerated growth rates. 
Other important measures for development of infrastructure are creation of 
special purpose vehicle to finance infrastructure, rapid infrastructure development 
through PPP and liberal, transparent and investor-friendly FDI policy wherein 
FDI up to 100 per cent is allowed under automatic route for most of the sectors 
with restrictions in few sectors.

Delay in Implementing Government Scheme 
†3575 PROF. ALKA BALRAM KSHATRIYA: Will the PRIME 
MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that it takes too much time in completing 
Government schemes due to several reasons; 
(b) the reasons behind this delay; and 
(c) the steps taken by Government to remove these shortcomings? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M. V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) and (b) While every effort is made for 
timely implementation of various scheme s, there have been several probable 
factors reported for slow progress, inter alia, delay in clearances from various 
agencies; law and order problem in certain States; procedural delays; inadequate 
provision of funds; institutional capacity of implementing agencies, non-
receipt/late receipt of the proposals from the State Governments as well as 
utilization certificates; delays in releasing matching share by State Government 
and recruitment and training process. 
(c) Several steps have been taken from time to time to remove these 
constraints, such as creating monitoring and evaluation mechanisms at 
different levels of Central and State Government as part of the programme 
guidelines; carrying out evaluation to a sses the effectiveness of the delivery 
systems and impact of the programme/ schemes by programme Evaluation 
Organization of Planning Commission;  recently introdu ced practice of 
placing 'Outcome Budget' of Central Ministries/Departments before the 
Parliament every year, and half yearly performance review of the Plan schemes 
of Central Ministries/ Departments. These measures are expected to ensure better 
coordination within arms of the Government.

Alarming Increase in slum and BPL population 
3631. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that population of slums in urban areas and 
209 

RAJYA SABHA [18 May, 2006] 
Below Poverty ILine population of urban areas of the country is increasing 
alarmingly; 
(b) if so, the concrete steps poposed to be taken by Central 
Government in regard to development of this population and to bring 
them to the main stream; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that so-called development schemes of Central 
Government for the improvement in the lives of these population are all failures 
due to improper implementation and half-baked planning, embezzlement of 
money; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the steps proposed to be taken thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
The Town & Country Planning Organization (TCPO) conducted a one time 
study on Slums in 1995-96 and brought out a report titled "A Compendium on 
Indian Slums-1996". According to this report, the slum population of the 
country, which was estimated to the 462.608 lakhs in 1991, is projected to be 
618.258 lakhs during 2001. However, as per the estimation of Planning 
Commission, the number of persons living Below Poverty Line has declined 
from 56.4 per cent in 1973-74 to 27.1 percent in 1999-2000. 
(b) For integrated development of slums through projects for providing 
shelter, basic services and other civic amenities and with a view to provide 
utilities to the urban poor in select 63 cities a Sub-Mission on Basic Services to 
the Urban Poor (BSUP) has been launched on 3rd December, 2005. In the 
remaining cities/towns an Integrated Housing & Slum Development Programme 
(IHSDP) has also been launched on 3rd December 2005. IHSDP has subsumed 
ValmikiAmbedkarAwas Yojana (VAMBAY) and National Slum Development 
Programme (NSDP). The targeted beneficiaries are slum dwellers/Urban 
Poor/EWS/LIG categories. 
In order to ameliorate the living conditions of the Urban Poor, Ministry of 
Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation is implementing an employment 
oriented urban poverty alleviation programme named Swarna Jayanti Shahari 
Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), on all India basis with effect from 1.12.1997. The 
Scheme is funded in proportion of 75:25 between Centre and the States. The 
SJSRY strives to provide gainful employment 
210 

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
to the urban unemployed or under-employed poor through (i) encouraging the 
setting up of Self-employment ventures by those who have not studied beyond 9th 
standard and (ii) provision of wage employment by utilizing their labour for 
construction of socially and economically useful public assets. 
(c) No, Sir. 
(d) In view of the (c) above, question does not arise. 
Poverty alleviation schemes 
3632. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN:  Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of Centrally implemented/sponsored poverty alleviation 
schemes under execution now; 
(b) whether any survey has been conducted in the recent times to 
ascertain the impact of these schemes in poverty alleviation; and 
(c) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) 
Ministry of Urban Employment and Poverty Alleviation is implementing on 
all India basis, an employment oriented urban poverty alleviation programme 
namely Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), with effect from 
1.12.1997. The Scheme strives to provide gainful employment to the urban 
unemployed and underemployed poor through firstly, encouraging the setting up 
of self-employment ventures by those who have not studied beyond 9th 
standard and, secondly, by providing wage employment by utilizing their labour 
for construction of socially and economically useful public assets. 
(b) and (c) All India evaluation of  Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rozgar 
Yojana (SJSRY) has been carried out recently by the Human Settlement 
Management Institute (HSMI), New Delhi. The major findings of the 
evaluation study are as under:— 
* Good impact in facilitating employment is observed in all the 
States. 
* Majority of the beneficiaries who were imparted skill training fall 
under the age group of 18-30 years. 
211 

RAJYASABHA [18 May, 2006] 
* Loan approval by banks in majority of cases in South and East India 
took lesser time than in the North & West India. 
* A good percentage of beneficiaries are having a decent earning from 
the SJSRY activities. 
* Women groups market their products on their own. and do not 
require any middleman for marketing except in some of the East & 
North Eastern States where majority of groups require middlemen 
for marketing. 
* The formation of DWCUAgroups has had a possitive impact on the 
women members as their desire and confidence for getting self-
employed has increased. This has led to increase in income and savings 
thereby improving their health, education and social prestige. 
* Thrift and Credit Societies (TCSs) are very active in organizing 
Health Camps, in providing assistance in making ration cards and in 
getting local children into primary schools enrolled. These have also 
been very effective in terms of promoting small savings and petty 
business, promoting group solidarity, resolving social and family 
discords and facilitating children's education. 
* Majority of the wage labourers under Urban Wage component of the 
scheme are employed for less than 3 months on an average and non 
sustainable employment keeps them in the BPL status. 
* Bank officials highlighted, inter-alia, inadequate skiil training, 
wrong choice of projects, non viability of the projects, lack of 
adequate publicity as the major reasons for non achievement of 
physical targets by some of the States.

Working of Games/Sports Associations 
3635. DR. K. MALAISAMY: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS         
AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) the prime purpose of Games/Sports Association prevailing at various 
levels in our country and their coordination and control mechanism; 
(b) whether it is a fact that many of such  associations are in existence in 
name-sake without doing much service and activities and some of such 
associations are manned by a few vested/political interests doing very little; 
and 
(c) would there not be a way out to get rid of such elements and 
introduce right persons for the right task? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKARAIYAR): (a) The basic purpose of  Games/Sports Associations at 
various levels is to promote the Games/Sports in their domain. These 
Associations are autonomous and function as per their rules and regulations 
and those of their national/international Bodies concerned. 
(b) and (c) Since 'sports' figures in the 'State List' of the Constitution, the 
Central Government neither deal with the Sports Associations working at 
District/State level nor have the mandate to legislate on any sports matter. 
The Central Government supplements the efforts of the National Sports 
Federations (NSFs) by providing fina ncial assistance for training & 
participation in International sports events abroad, organization of 
international tournaments in India; holding of national championships at sub-
junior, junior and senior level, training/coaching of national teams/ sports 
persons under Indian and foreign coaches with requisite technical, scientific and 
nutrition support. Since NSFs are autonomous registered bodies, the 
Government of India does not interfere in the electoral process of these bodies.

National Sports Development Fund 
3639. SHRI N. R. GOVINDARAJAR : Will the Minister of YOUTH 
AFFAIRS AND SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have created any National Sports 
Development Fund for promotion of sports and games in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have formulated any. policy for spotting 
talented sportspersons in rural areas; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) The National Sports Development Fund 
(NSDF) was created by the Government in 1998 with the aim of promoting sports 
in general and specific sports disciplines & individual sportspersons in particular 
for achieving excellence at the national and international level. The Fund 
envisages mobilizing financial resources from statutory bodies created under the 
Act of Parliament or the State Legislatures, the United Nations and its 
associated bodies, other International Organizations, private and public 
corporate sectors, trusts, societies and individuals. There is a provision for 
matching contributions from the Government. The contributions received for 
the Fund have the facility of 100% tax exemption. 
220 

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) and (d) Under the scheme of 'Incentives for Promotion of Sports 
Activities' of this Ministry, Rural Sports Programme is one of the 
components under which rural sports competitions/tournaments are 
organized at Block, District, State and National levels. Block level 
Tournaments are to be funded by the State Govt./UT Administration. 
However, NGOs including Nehru Yuva Kendra Sangathana are also 
provided assistance for holding local rural tournaments at district level. The 
Government provides grants to the State Governments through the Sports 
Authority of India (SAI) for organizi ng District, State and National level 
tournaments. District level tournaments are organized by State Governments 
and State level tournaments are organized by SAI in association with the 
State/UT. National level tournaments are organized by SAI in various States by 
rotation.

SHRI SHARAD ANANTRAO JOSHI (Maharashtra): Thank you very 
much, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am sorry I could not follow the whole debate 
because from 3 o'clock, we had a meeting of the Standing Advisory Committee 
where we had to finalise a report and I had to leave the House for that 
purpose. But, since I came, I have heard some speeches and, ! think, I have 
generally followed the trend of the discussion that has taken place here. 
The situation, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, is extremely grave. I feel like 
howling and crying out when I read reports of 7-10 farmers committing suicide 
everyday in the region of Vidarbha itself. But howling and crying and histrionics 
and making speeches with raised voices  does not yield the result or any 
solution. What is necessary is to sit down coolly, make an analysis of 
309 

RAJYA SABHA [18 May, 2006] 
the situation, diagnose the disease and find a proper remedy. As far as the farmers' 
suicides are concerned, I think, I have in this House spoken at least a dozen times 
on this subject. But the subject has co me up again. By now there is a general 
broad agreement on the real cause of t he farmers' suicides. In the early reports 
prepared by the experts it was said that suicides always take place because of a 
complex of various factors. It is never a sing le factor that results in suicides. It was 
said that farmers who commit suicide have some addiction, they possibly have 
some illnesses, diseases that make them despair of the life. But finally everybody 
came to the conclusion that the most prox imate cause of all suicides was the fact 
that the farmers were heavily in debt and there was a pressure brought from the -
creditors who might be a private moneylen der or more often a cooperative credit 
society and that they use methods of reco very, which are humiliating, insulting and 
that resulted in loss of prestige to the fa rmers for whom living in dignity in that 
village is a very important consideration. So, the final stage, the penultimate stage 
is the humiliation heaped on the farmers bec ause of the kind of recoveries that 
were being imposed by the creditors. Why did it come to this stage? The reasons 
are very clear. It was C. Subramanium who poi nted out for the first time that Indian 
agriculture was a losing proposition because the farmers did not get the prices that 
would cover their cost of production. This was a diagnosis made by C. 
Subramanium himself. The farmers movements in the last 20 years have been 
giving enough evidence of this, and I would say today that except for a few 
enlightened farmers, who apart from agriculture also do some processing, also do 
some exporting or have some kind of an associated activity with agriculture, and 
are possibly able to meet their expenses, agriculture per se, agriculture by itself, is 
necessarily a losing proposition. In fact  in the movements, Sir, we do tell the 
farmers, "Do not be shy of admitting that you are in debt. If you are in debt, it only 
means that you are honest. It is only a dishonest farmer who can be without debt. 
All honest farmers are in trouble today in this country." Why did this happen, I' do 
not want to go into all the controversies. The matter is very clear. We know and it 
has been admitted by the Minister for Commerce, it » has been admitted by the 
Minister for Agriculture that even today the Indian agriculture is working under 
conditions of negative aggr egate measure of support which in common parlance 
means that the farmer in India gets much lesser price than he would have got in a 
market where there was no intervention by the Government - in a hypothetical^ free 
market. In all the countries like Japan, Europe and USA the farmers get much more 
than

[18 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
what they would have got in a free market. In India farmers get much less than 
they would have got in a free market because of the various restrictive policies 
including the Essential Commodities Act imposed by the Government, the 
various bans on exports, dumping operations carried out, as is being carried 
out right now, we purchase wheat at a hi gher price and bring it in our market 
and dispose it of at a lower price. We have restrictions on the movement of 
agricultural commodities from one Stat e to another, from one district to 
another. We have restrictions on the pr ocessing, we have restrictions on the 
storage and all this results in the fact  that the farmers are never able to 
recover the cost of production even in years when the nature is favourable and 
the crops are good. Now you will get a clue as to why is it that the cotton 
producing farmers have a greater incidence of suicides than, for example, the 
sugarcane producing farmers. It is not that the sugarcane producing farmers 
are more brave, it is not  that the cotton producing farmers are.cowards. The 
fact is, and you will see it in the st atement that was submitted by Pranab 
Mukherjeeji as Minister of Commerce to the WTO, that in 1986-1989, cotton 
had a negative subsidy co-efficient of 110 per cent which meant that if the cost 
of production of cotton was Rs. 210, t he farmers were not able to get more 
than Rs.100. That was the position of cotton. On the other hand, in the case of 
sugarcane there was a positive AMS, i.e. if the cost of production was Rs. 100, 
the sugarcane producers were able to get  about Rs. 108. Sir, that is the 
reason why the cotton-producing farmers have a greater incidence of suicides. 
Before I left, I heard some analysis of what kind of farmers commit suicide and 
I would like to make some things very clear. There is very little incidence of 
suicides amongst farmers who do not own any land. The landless labourers 
don't commit suicides because they are better off in today's situation than the 
land-holding farmers. The land-holding farmers, incur the risk of natural 
calamities and of Governmental interventions, while the landless labourers 
who earn only wages, but they are fixed wages and nothing is cut from that.

very serious problem that we are facing in the rural areas. I would like to 
stress upon only two or three points. Actually we have to find out the actual

are not at all worried about the price of  a particular product in the industrial

And, the producer has got the right to fix the price. The producer can preserve 
the product and he can give it at appr opriate time so that his cost of the 
production can be met and he can also get more profit if he can preserve 
product for a particular favourable ma rket. But, the agriculturists alone, the 
peasants alone, have got no control over the cost of their production and also 
the price of their produce. They cannot  demand higher price for this much of 
cost, therefore, you have to pay this much of cost. They are not in a position 
to fix their cost, but at the same time , they are, somehow, meeting the cost 
also. It is in the hands of rain god. The rain has to come at appropriate time

surplus water or if there is any flood, then nobody is going to protect them. If 
there is no water at all, dr ought situation is there, even then, nobody is there 
to protect them. The interest rates are go ing up. There is short-term relief. As 
an economist has suggested, there will be relief for the co-operative loans, but
